title: Sumerian flood story as the source of Noah

tellings.quote: if you read the Epic of Gilgamesh the atrasis and then you compare the flood story it's like literally almost identical to Genesis
Throw down the house, build a ship,
Carry grain of every kind into the ship.
The cattle of the field, the beasts of the field, all handicraftsmen I made them go up into it.
The storm raged, and the cyclone overwhelmed the land.
The mountain of Nisir held the ship, it let it not move.
I brought out a dove and let her go free.
I brought out a swallow and let her go free.
I brought out a raven and let her go free.
She ate, she pecked in the ground, she croaked, she came not back.

plain: A researcher named Matt LaCroix says on the show that the flood stories of ancient Mesopotamia, in the Epic of Gilgamesh and the older poem Atrahasis, are "almost identical to Genesis," which would make them the source of Noah's ark. In E. A. Wallis Budge's 1920 translation of the epic's eleventh tablet, the survivor Utnapishtim is told to "throw down the house, build a ship," loads it with grain, cattle and craftsmen, rides out a storm until "the mountain of Nisir held the ship," and then sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven, which "came not back." The epic names neither Noah nor Genesis: the comparison is LaCroix's own.

discussion.by: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)
discussion.text: The words are from E. A. Wallis Budge's translation (The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, 1920) of the Eleventh Tablet of the Assyrian version, in which Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamish of the flood. The comparison with Genesis is the teller's: the epic names neither Noah nor Genesis.
